items.title: Three systems: presidential, mixed president/PM, parliamentary
items.body:
Every democracy has to answer one question: **where does the government's power to act come from, and who can take it away?** The US, Poland and India give three different answers, and those answers explain a good share of this week's news.

**Presidential: the United States.** Americans elect the president separately from Congress, for a fixed four-year term. The president is both head of state and head of government and picks a cabinet whose members cannot sit in Congress and do not need its confidence. Congress cannot dismiss a president over policy. The only route is impeachment: the House accuses, and the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict. The two branches are elected on different calendars and can be held by rival parties. That is the **separation of powers** in its purest form.

> The US Constitution was drafted at the [#Constitutional Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Convention_(United_States)) in Philadelphia in 1787 and took effect in 1789.

**Parliamentary: India.** Indians vote only for their member of the Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament. The prime minister is whoever can command a majority there, and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it: if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole government falls. Ministers must be members of Parliament, or become one within six months. The president, currently [@Droupadi Murmu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Droupadi_Murmu), is chosen indirectly by an electoral college of MPs and state legislators and, under Article 74, acts on the ministers' advice. Executive power and the legislative majority are **fused**: a prime minister such as [@Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi) stays in office for as long as he keeps the House behind him.

> India's Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, the date now marked as Republic Day.

**Mixed: Poland.** Poland sits in between. Its president is directly elected for five years and holds real tools: he can veto bills (the Sejm needs a three-fifths majority to override), send laws to the Constitutional Tribunal, and plays a leading role in defence and foreign policy. Day-to-day government, though, belongs to the prime minister and the Council of Ministers, who need the confidence of the Sejm. The Sejm can remove a government only by a **constructive vote of no confidence**, which must name a new prime minister in the same vote, so a majority cannot topple a cabinet without agreeing on a replacement. Political scientists disagree on the label: some call Poland semi-presidential, others a parliamentary system with an unusually strong president.

> The current Constitution was approved by referendum in May 1997 and took effect on 17 October 1997.

Each design has a typical weakness. A presidential system risks **gridlock**: when the president and Congress belong to rival parties, neither can remove the other, so they bargain or stall. A parliamentary system risks **instability**: lose your majority and you lose power, which makes coalition partners very important. Poland can face both at once. When the president and the prime minister come from rival camps, a situation called **cohabitation**, the president's veto can block laws even though the government controls the Sejm.

That is Poland's situation today. Prime Minister [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk) depends on a four-party coalition in the Sejm, so a split inside one partner, Polska 2050, is a threat to his government. President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki), who won the [#2025 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Polish_presidential_election) with the backing of the opposition Law and Justice party, decides whether to sign the coalition's bills. Compare the US: in the [#2026 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_elections) on 3 November, voters choose the whole House and a third of the Senate, but whatever the result, [@Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) stays president until January 2029. In India or Poland, losing a parliamentary majority would mean a new government.

Later lessons build on this one: who is head of state versus head of government (Lesson 3), how each legislature works (Lesson 5), and how vetoes and overrides play out (Lesson 7).

items.example: Two cases show what "confidence" means in practice. After the [#2023 Polish parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Polish_parliamentary_election), President [@Andrzej Duda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Duda) first reappointed [@Mateusz Morawiecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mateusz_Morawiecki) of Law and Justice, the largest single party, even though it lacked a majority. His [#third cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Cabinet_of_Mateusz_Morawiecki), sworn in on 27 November, lost its confidence vote in the Sejm on 11 December 2023. That same day the Sejm elected [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk), whose government was sworn in two days later. In India, after the [#1996 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Indian_general_election), [@Atal Bihari Vajpayee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atal_Bihari_Vajpayee) became prime minister as leader of the largest party but resigned after 13 days, before a confidence vote he expected to lose. Nothing like this can happen in Washington: a president whose party loses Congress keeps the job.
items.inTheNews: Polska 2050's split tests whether [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk) keeps the Sejm majority his government depends on, the parliamentary half of Poland's system, while the abortion bills heading to President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) show the presidential half. In the US, the [#3 November midterms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_elections) will reshape Congress but cannot change who is president.

check.q: Polish coalition partners fall out and a majority of the Sejm now dislikes the government, but they cannot agree on who should replace Tusk. What happens?
options: The government falls automatically
The government stays, because a constructive no-confidence vote must name a successor
The President dismisses the Prime Minister
New elections are held at once
check.explain: Poland's no-confidence vote is constructive: the Sejm must elect a new prime minister in the same vote, so a majority that cannot agree on a replacement cannot remove the government.

check.q: Which change would end a sitting Indian government but not a sitting US administration?
options: Losing a majority in the lower house

check.explain: India's government must keep the Lok Sabha's confidence. A US president keeps office for a fixed term even if their party loses the House.

check.q: Why do some scholars call Poland semi-presidential rather than simply parliamentary?
options: Its president appoints all judges alone
Its president is directly elected and has real powers such as a veto that needs three-fifths to override
Its prime minister is directly elected
It has no prime minister
check.explain: A directly elected president with a meaningful veto and a role in defence and foreign policy sits alongside a government responsible to the Sejm, which is the mark of a mixed system.

items.recallQ: Why can a US president stay in office after his party loses the midterms, while a Polish or Indian prime minister who loses a parliamentary majority usually cannot?
items.recallA: The US president is elected separately for a fixed term and does not need Congress's confidence; only impeachment can remove him. Polish and Indian governments are responsible to the lower house, so losing its support (through a no-confidence vote, constructive in Poland's case) brings the government down.

items.body:
Lesson 1 showed that each country splits power differently. A **veto** is where that split becomes concrete: it is the moment one branch says no to a law the legislature has already passed. All three countries give their president a veto, but its strength depends on two things: **how big a majority the legislature needs to override it**, and **whether the president can simply run out the clock**.

**United States: strong veto, hard override.** Under Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution, every bill goes to the president, who has ten days (Sundays excluded) to sign it or return it to Congress with objections. Congress can override only with a **two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate**, a bar that one party rarely clears on its own. That is why overrides are rare: of about 2,600 vetoes since 1789, Congress has overridden 112. There is also a **pocket veto**: if Congress adjourns during the ten days, an unsigned bill simply dies and cannot be overridden. In practice, the *threat* of a veto shapes bills long before they reach the president's desk.

> The first presidential veto was cast by [@George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington) in 1792, against a bill dividing House seats among the states.

**Poland: a veto aimed at the government.** Article 122 of the 1997 Constitution gives the president 21 days. He can sign; he can send the law to the Constitutional Tribunal; or he can veto it and send it back to the Sejm, but he cannot do both. To override, the Sejm needs **three-fifths of the votes cast, with at least half of its 460 deputies present**. The Senate has no role in the override. Because Polish governments usually rest on a slim majority, three-fifths is often out of reach. That matters most during **cohabitation**, when the president and the government come from rival camps. Since taking office in August 2025, [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) has vetoed about fifty laws passed by [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk)'s coalition, a record for any Polish president, and the Sejm has not overridden one. Supporters see a needed check on the government; critics say the veto has become a second, unelected programme for governing. The government often responds by rewriting a vetoed bill to win the president's signature, or by acting through ministerial regulations, which need no signature.

**India: a weak veto, but a long pause.** Under Article 111, India's president can sign a bill, withhold assent, or return it (except a money bill) to Parliament for reconsideration once. If both houses pass it again, by an ordinary majority, the president **must** sign. Formally, this is the weakest veto of the three. Its real force comes from what the Constitution leaves out: **there is no deadline**. In 1986 President [@Zail Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zail_Singh) let a bill on intercepting postal mail sit unsigned until it was dropped, India's best-known pocket veto. The same question arises in the states, where centrally appointed **governors** can sit on state bills under Article 200. In the [#State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Tamil_Nadu_v._Governor_of_Tamil_Nadu) case of April 2025, the Supreme Court set deadlines. In November 2025, a five-judge bench answering a [#presidential reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_re:_Assent,_Withholding_or_Reservation_of_Bills_by_the_Governor_and_the_President_of_India) said courts cannot impose fixed timelines, but added that governors may not delay bills indefinitely.

> Under Article 143, the president can ask the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion on any question of law. This is called a presidential reference.

The pattern: the US veto is strong because overrides need a supermajority in two chambers; Poland's is strong because coalition governments seldom reach three-fifths; India's is weak on paper but can still stall a bill through delay. When you read that a veto "blocked" a reform, ask what override threshold applies and whether the government has the votes to reach it.

Killing a bill by not acting on it: formally in the US when Congress adjourns, and in practice in India, where there is no deadline.

items.example: In 1973 Congress passed the **War Powers Resolution**, which requires the president to report to Congress within 48 hours of sending troops into hostilities and to withdraw them after 60 days without congressional approval. President [@Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon) vetoed it, arguing that it unconstitutionally limited his powers as commander-in-chief. The [#War Powers Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Powers_Resolution) became law anyway. On 7 November 1973, exactly 53 years ago today, the House and the Senate both cleared the two-thirds bar, helped by Nixon's weakness during the [#Watergate scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal). The case shows what an override takes in the US: members of the president's own party had to vote against him. It also shows how a veto keeps shaping a law after it passes. Presidents of both parties have since said the resolution is unconstitutional and have often reported to Congress only "consistent with" it, never conceding that it binds them.
items.inTheNews: S&P cut Poland's rating outlook to negative partly because presidential vetoes by [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) limit the government's fiscal plans, and Finance Minister [@Andrzej Domański](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Doma%C5%84ski) blamed the president. In the US, House Democrats are planning votes for next year that, without two-thirds majorities, could not survive a veto by [@Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump).

check.q: Poland's ruling coalition has a clear majority in the Sejm but well under three-fifths of the seats. What happens to a law the president vetoes?
options: It becomes law once the Senate approves it again
It fails unless opposition deputies help reach three-fifths of the votes cast
It goes automatically to the Constitutional Tribunal
The coalition can pass it again by a simple majority after 30 days
check.explain: Article 122 requires three-fifths of votes cast (with half the deputies present) and gives the Senate no role. A coalition with a bare majority needs opposition votes, or enough opposition absences, to override.

check.q: Why is India's presidential veto often described as weak on paper but still capable of stalling a bill?
options: Because the Rajya Sabha can block any override
Because a two-thirds majority is needed to override it
Because Parliament can override it by simple re-passage, but the Constitution sets no deadline for the president to act
Because the Supreme Court must approve every vetoed bill
check.explain: Under Article 111 a re-passed bill must be signed, so the formal veto only delays. The lack of a time limit lets a president, or a governor for state bills, simply not act.

check.q: A US bill reaches the president eight days before Congress adjourns for the year. The president neither signs nor vetoes it. What happens?
options: It becomes law after ten days
It dies by pocket veto and cannot be overridden
It goes back to Congress for an override vote next session
The Supreme Court decides whether it takes effect
check.explain: If Congress adjourns within the ten-day window and so prevents the bill's return, the unsigned bill does not become law. With no returned veto, Congress has nothing to override.

items.recallQ: Why does the threshold for overriding a veto (two-thirds, three-fifths or a simple majority) matter so much for how powerful a president's veto really is?
items.recallA: The veto's real strength is the size of the majority needed to defeat it. The US two-thirds rule in both chambers and Poland's three-fifths rule usually mean the ruling side needs opposition votes, so a veto often kills a bill. In India a simple re-passage overrides the president, so his veto mainly delays a bill, and delay without a deadline is its main source of power.

items.body:
This week had only one new lesson, Lesson 7, **Vetoes and overrides**, but it was the right one for the week's news, and it rests on Lesson 1, **Three systems** from late October. Put together, the two lessons explain most of what happened in Washington and Warsaw.

**Lesson 1 asked who answers to whom.** The US president is elected separately for a fixed term; Polish and Indian governments live or die by a majority in the lower house. That is why the [#2026 United States elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_elections) changed Congress but not the White House. Networks project that Democrats won both chambers, yet [@Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) stays in office until January 2029. In Poland or India, a defeat of that size in the lower house would have meant a new government.

**Lesson 7 asked what happens when the branches disagree.** From 3 January the US returns to divided government, and the veto becomes the president's main shield. Democrats look set to hold roughly 54 Senate seats and over 250 House seats, well short of the 67 and 290 needed for a two-thirds override. So bills they pass next year can still be stopped by one signature withheld. Before then comes the lame-duck session that opens on 9 November, with the old Republican majorities facing an 11 December funding deadline.

> The [#Twentieth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twentieth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution), ratified in 1933, moved the start of a new Congress to 3 January, shortening lame-duck sessions.

**Poland shows the same tools under a mixed system.** President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) and Prime Minister [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk) come from rival camps, which is cohabitation. On 6 November the Senate sent him the abortion bills, the resubmitted tax reform and the judges' act, starting his 21-day clock. Because Tusk's coalition lacks three-fifths of the Sejm, a veto would likely stand. S&P cited those vetoes when it cut Poland's outlook to negative, and the finance minister blamed the president. Opinions divide along party lines: one side sees a check on the government, the other an obstacle to it.

But cohabitation is not only conflict. Many of the Polish president's acts need the prime minister's **countersignature**, a feature of the mixed system from Lesson 1. This week Nawrocki appointed four members of the National Bank of Poland's board after Tusk countersigned, ending an eight-month standoff. Each side holds a key the other needs, so deals are possible.

> Poland's current constitution was adopted by the National Assembly in April 1997 and approved in a referendum on 25 May 1997.

**India was quiet on these themes this week**, which is itself a lesson: with a stable majority in the Lok Sabha and a president who seldom resists, the Indian veto is mainly a delay tool, used, as with [@Zail Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zail_Singh) in 1986, by not acting.

The common thread: power depends less on what the constitution grants than on the numbers. Ask who controls each branch, and how big a majority is needed to beat a veto.

check.q: Democrats are projected to win both houses of Congress. Why does Trump remain president, while a similar loss would likely end a Polish or Indian government?
options: Because US midterms do not count until certified in January
Because the US president is elected separately for a fixed term and does not need Congress's confidence
Because the Senate must first vote to remove him
Because the Supreme Court decides whether he stays
check.explain: In a presidential system the executive does not depend on a legislative majority. Polish and Indian governments must keep the lower house's confidence (Lesson 1).

check.q: From January, Democrats will hold about 54 Senate seats and more than 250 House seats. What does that mean for bills Trump vetoes?
options: They can override any veto by simple majority
They can override only in the House
They will usually need Republican votes, because two-thirds of both chambers is required
Vetoed bills go automatically to the Supreme Court
check.explain: An override needs 67 senators and 290 representatives if all seats are filled and voting. A narrow majority falls short, so the veto usually holds (Lesson 7).

check.q: Nawrocki appointed new NBP board members only after Tusk countersigned. What does this show about Poland's mixed system?
options: The prime minister can veto any law
Many presidential acts need the prime minister's countersignature, so rivals must sometimes cooperate
The president appoints the whole government alone
The Sejm must approve every presidential decision
check.explain: Countersignature ties the president to the government for many acts. In cohabitation it gives each side leverage, which can produce deals as well as standoffs.

check.q: Why is India's presidential veto described as weaker than Poland's, even though both presidents can return a bill?
options: India's president cannot return any bill
An Indian bill re-passed by an ordinary majority must be signed, while Poland requires three-fifths of the Sejm
Poland's president can dissolve the Sejm after any veto
India requires a referendum to override
check.explain: India's Article 111 veto only delays; Poland's Article 122 veto needs a three-fifths Sejm vote to overcome, which coalition governments often lack.

items.recallQ: In a lame-duck session, why might an outgoing majority rush to pass laws, and why does that matter less in Poland or India?
items.recallA: Between the November election and 3 January, the old US Congress still sits, so the losing majority can pass bills before it hands over control. Poland and India have no comparable stretch: after an election the old parliament stops legislating, the new Sejm or Lok Sabha takes over, and the outgoing government serves only as caretaker until a new one is formed.

items.body:
Lesson 1 sorted the three countries by system. This lesson looks at the documents that set those systems up, and at the hardest question any constitution must answer: **how can it be changed?** A constitution is higher law. Ordinary statutes must fit inside it, and courts (Lesson 8) can strike down those that don't. So the amendment rule decides how far any winning majority can rewrite the rules of the game on its own.

**United States: the oldest, and the hardest to change.** Written at the [#Constitutional Convention (United States)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Convention_(United_States)) in 1787 and in force since 1789, the US Constitution is short, about 4,500 words without amendments. Article V sets a double supermajority: an amendment must be proposed by **two-thirds of both the House and the Senate** (or by a convention requested by two-thirds of the states, a route never used) and then ratified by **three-quarters of the states**, today 38 of 50. The president has no formal role. Only 27 amendments have passed, ten of them at once as the [#United States Bill of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bill_of_Rights) in 1791. The [#Equal Rights Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Rights_Amendment) cleared Congress in 1972 but fell short of 38 states before its deadline. Because formal change is so hard, much US constitutional change happens through Supreme Court interpretation instead.

> Drafted largely by [@James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison), the Constitution was signed on 17 September 1787 in Philadelphia's Independence Hall.

**Poland: a young constitution with a high bar.** Poland's current Constitution was adopted by the National Assembly in April 1997 and approved in the [#1997 Polish constitutional referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Polish_constitutional_referendum). Under Article 235, an amendment can be proposed by a fifth of deputies (92), the Senate or the president. The Sejm must pass it by **two-thirds of the votes cast, with at least half of its 460 members present**, and the Senate by an absolute majority within 60 days. Changes to Chapter I (the Republic), Chapter II (rights) or Chapter XII (amendment itself) can be put to a referendum if the president, the Senate or a fifth of deputies ask. The president must then sign within 21 days: unlike ordinary laws (Lesson 7), an amendment cannot be vetoed. The text has changed only twice, in 2006 and 2009. Since no camp has held two-thirds of the Sejm, fights over the system play out through ordinary laws and court rulings instead.

> Poland's first written constitution, the [#Constitution of 3 May 1791](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_3_May_1791), is often called Europe's first modern codified constitution (Lesson 27).

**India: the longest, most amended, but with a limit.** The [#Constituent Assembly of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituent_Assembly_of_India) drafted the world's longest national constitution between 1946 and 1949, with [@B. R. Ambedkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._R._Ambedkar) chairing its drafting committee. Article 368 offers several routes. Some provisions, such as creating a new state, change by an ordinary law. Most need a **special majority in each house**: a majority of total membership *and* two-thirds of members present and voting. Provisions touching federalism, such as states' representation or the division of powers, also need approval by **half the state legislatures**. The president must give assent. Because the text is so detailed, many policy changes require amendments, and Parliament has passed 106. But in [#Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kesavananda_Bharati_v._State_of_Kerala) (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's **basic structure**, so even an amendment can be struck down. That limit was soon tested by the sweeping [#Forty-second Amendment of the Constitution of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty-second_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_of_India), passed during [#The Emergency (India)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Emergency_(India)) (Lesson 44).

> The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.

**What the bar measures.** The US rule demands agreement across both chambers and most of the states, so it is almost never met. Poland's two-thirds usually needs the government and the opposition to agree, which in today's polarized Sejm means stalemate. India's two-thirds is high but reachable for a large governing majority, so Parliament amends often, and the courts became the brake. In each country, the amendment rule shows whose consent a lasting change really needs.

items.example: In April 2026 India's government brought the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to the Lok Sabha. That is a clear majority, and enough for any ordinary law, but Article 368 demands two-thirds of those present and voting, 352 here, so the bill failed by 54 votes. Lesson 1 sorted the three countries into presidential, mixed and parliamentary systems. This lesson zooms in on the idea underneath that sorting. Every state needs two jobs done. The **head of state** embodies the country: a symbol of continuity who receives ambassadors, signs laws, awards honours and leads the nation in mourning. The **head of government** runs the country day to day: setting policy, directing ministers and answering to voters or parliament. The question is whether one person holds both jobs or two people share them.

**United States: one person, both hats.** Article II gives all executive power to the president, so [@Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) is at once the national symbol and the chief policymaker. He greets foreign leaders and lays wreaths, but he also commands the armed forces, picks the cabinet and decides strategy, such as declaring the Iran war "effectively" over. The upside is clear accountability: there is one person to praise or blame. The downside is that a deeply partisan figure also has to be the unifying symbol, and many Americans find it hard to see their opponent's president as theirs too.

> The title "Mr. President" was settled in 1789, when Congress rejected grander titles for [@George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington).

**India: a symbolic president, a ruling prime minister.** India copied the British model. The **President** (Rashtrapati), today [@Droupadi Murmu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Droupadi_Murmu), is head of state. She is chosen indirectly for five years by an electoral college of MPs and state legislators, not by voters. Under Article 74 she must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers, led by the **Prime Minister** (Pradhan Mantri), today [@Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi). Real power follows the Lok Sabha majority. The president keeps a few genuine choices: who to invite to form a government when no party has a majority, and the right to send advice back once for reconsideration.

> India's first president, [@Rajendra Prasad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rajendra_Prasad), took office on 26 January 1950, the day the Constitution came into force.

**Poland: two real players.** Poland sits in between. The **President** (Prezydent RP), today [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki), is elected directly by voters for five years, at most two terms. That popular mandate gives him real weight: he can veto laws (Lesson 7), send them to the Constitutional Tribunal, nominate the prime minister, and he is commander-in-chief of the armed forces. But the government is run by the **Prime Minister** (Prezes Rady Ministrów), today [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk), who answers to the Sejm. Most of the president's official acts need the prime minister's **countersignature** (kontrasygnata); the 1997 Constitution lists the exceptions, called prerogatives, which he may use alone.

> Poland restored the presidency in 1989 as part of the [#Polish Round Table Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Round_Table_Agreement); the first popular election followed in 1990.

When the president and prime minister come from rival camps, as Nawrocki (backed by PiS) and Tusk (Civic Coalition) do now, the French call it **cohabitation**. It produces constant friction: vetoes, disputes over ambassadors and judges, and competing claims to speak for Poland abroad. Political scientists disagree on whether this is a design flaw or a useful brake on whichever side controls the Sejm.

The split also explains moments like this week's. After the Kraków shooting, the president's job as head of state is to embody national grief, award honours and stand above party; the prime minister's job is to run the response through the Interior Ministry and police. Seeing them walk side by side was notable precisely because their daily relationship is so adversarial.

The [#Forty-second Amendment of the Constitution of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty-second_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_of_India) (1976) then made ministerial advice explicitly binding. After Gandhi lost the 1977 election, the [#Forty-fourth Amendment of the Constitution of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty-fourth_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_of_India) (1978) let the president return advice once, and required a cabinet decision in writing before any emergency. Lesson 3 separated the head of state from the head of government. This lesson looks at the team the head of government leads: the **executive**, the ministers who run departments and turn policy into action. In all three countries that team is often called "the cabinet", but how it is built, who can join it and who can remove its members differ sharply, and those differences explain a lot of this week's news.

**United States: the president's advisers.** The Constitution never uses the word "cabinet". Article II gives executive power to the president alone and lets him ask the heads of departments for written opinions. Today the cabinet is the heads of the 15 executive departments plus officials the president chooses to add. The president nominates each secretary, and the Senate must confirm them by majority vote. Two rules make the American executive distinctive. First, secretaries cannot sit in Congress at the same time, so a senator picked for the cabinet must resign. Second, they serve at the president's pleasure: he can fire any of them at will, but Congress can remove one only through impeachment, a majority in the House and two-thirds in the Senate. That is why [@Thomas Massie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Massie)'s articles against Defense Secretary [@Pete Hegseth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Hegseth) mattered so little in practice: even a House majority could not have removed him without a Senate supermajority.

> The first executive departments, State, War and Treasury, were created by Congress in 1789 under President [@George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington).

**Poland: the Council of Ministers governs collectively.** In Poland the government is a body, the **Council of Ministers** (Rada Ministrów), led by the prime minister. Under Article 146 of the Constitution it runs domestic and foreign policy, and it holds every power not given to another state organ. Its formation is a three-step process. The president nominates a prime minister, who proposes ministers; within 14 days the new government must win a vote of confidence in the Sejm. If it fails, the Sejm picks its own candidate, and only after that does the choice return to the president. Ministers may also be MPs, and many are. The Sejm can remove a single minister through an individual vote of no confidence, which needs 69 deputies to propose it and an absolute majority of all 460 deputies to pass. Because the Council acts as a body, it adopts bills to send to parliament and issues regulations, as it did this week on nuclear siting and red tape.

> Reborn Poland's first government was formed in November 1918 under [@Jędrzej Moraczewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jędrzej_Moraczewski), days after independence.

**India: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.** India's **Union Council of Ministers** has three ranks: Cabinet ministers, who head major ministries and meet as the Cabinet; Ministers of State with independent charge; and junior Ministers of State. The president appoints all of them on the prime minister's advice. Article 75 sets two rules borrowed from Britain. Ministers must be members of Parliament, or become one within six months. And the Council is **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha: if it loses a confidence vote, the whole government falls, not one minister. Ministers who disagree in private are expected to defend Cabinet decisions in public or resign. A 2003 amendment caps the Council at 15% of the Lok Sabha, so no more than 81 ministers.

> India's first Union Cabinet was sworn in on 15 August 1947 under Prime Minister [@Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru).

**What the comparison shows.** The American cabinet is a set of advisers who answer to one boss, so Congress checks them mainly through confirmation, hearings and money. In Poland and India ministers sit inside the legislature and depend on its confidence, so parliament can bring them down without a trial. Poland adds a twist India lacks: the Sejm can target one minister, while India's rule is that ministers stand or fall together.

After the [#2023 Polish parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Polish_parliamentary_election), President [@Andrzej Duda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Duda) used the first step to nominate [@Mateusz Morawiecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mateusz_Morawiecki) of PiS, the largest single party, even though PiS lacked a majority. Lesson 4 showed that in Poland and India the government must keep the confidence of parliament, while in the US the cabinet answers only to the president. That raises the obvious next question: what exactly is that parliament? All three countries have **bicameral** legislatures, with two chambers, but the two chambers are far from equal partners in Poland and India, and almost perfectly equal in the US.

**United States: two equal houses.** Article I gives all federal lawmaking power to Congress. The **House of Representatives** has 435 members elected every two years from single-member districts drawn by population. The **Senate** has 100 members, two per state regardless of size, serving six-year terms, with a third elected every two years. That split came from the [#Connecticut Compromise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_Compromise) of 1787 between large and small states. Senators were chosen by state legislatures until the [#Seventeenth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution) made them directly elected in 1913. No bill becomes law unless both chambers pass the identical text, so a party that controls only one house can block almost everything. Each chamber also has its own jobs: the House starts tax bills and impeaches; the Senate confirms nominees, approves treaties by two-thirds and holds impeachment trials. Day to day, real power sits with party leaders chosen by each party's members, such as the Senate majority leader.

> Congress first met on 4 March 1789 at Federal Hall in New York City, and moved to Washington, D.C., in 1800.

**Poland: a strong Sejm and a reviewing Senate.** Poland's parliament has a lower house, the **Sejm**, with 460 deputies elected for four years by proportional representation from party lists, and an upper house, the **Senate** (Senat), with 100 senators elected at the same time in single-member districts where the top vote-getter wins. The two systems produce different results: a party with 35% of the vote gets at least a third of the Sejm, but can win far more or far fewer Senate seats depending on how its rivals split. The Sejm clearly dominates. Bills start there; the Senate has 30 days to accept, amend or reject them, and the Sejm can overturn any Senate change by an absolute majority of votes cast. Only the Sejm can bring down the government. The Sejm is run by its **Marshal** (Marszałek), currently [@Włodzimierz Czarzasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C5%82odzimierz_Czarzasty) under the coalition's rotation deal.

> The Sejm traces its start to the 1493 general assembly in Piotrków under King [@John I Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_Albert).

> The Senate, abolished in 1946, returned under the [#Polish Round Table Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Round_Table_Agreement); its first members were chosen in the [#1989 Polish parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Polish_parliamentary_election).

**India: the House of the People and the Council of States.** The **Lok Sabha** (House of the People) has 543 elected members chosen for up to five years by first-past-the-post in single-member constituencies; it can be dissolved early. The **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States) speaks for the federal side: up to 250 members, currently 233 elected by state legislatures in proportion to population plus 12 nominated by the President for expertise in fields like the arts and science. It is never dissolved; a third of its members retire every two years. The Lok Sabha is stronger in three ways. The government answers only to it. Money bills can start only there, and the Rajya Sabha can merely suggest changes within 14 days. And if the houses deadlock on an ordinary bill, the President can call a joint sitting, where the larger Lok Sabha usually prevails; this has happened only three times, most recently over the [#Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevention_of_Terrorism_Act,_2002). Still, a government without a Rajya Sabha majority must bargain for constitutional amendments, which need two-thirds in each house.

> The first Lok Sabha was constituted in April 1952, after the [#1951–52 Indian general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951%E2%80%9352_Indian_general_election).

**The pattern.** In the parliamentary systems the lower house makes and breaks governments, so the upper house becomes a chamber of review and delay. In the presidential US, neither chamber can remove the government, so both keep full veto power over legislation. That is why American elections for either chamber can reshape a whole presidency.

items.body:
Lesson 5 described the two chambers in each country. Today's question is what a proposal has to survive on its way from an idea to a binding law. The short answer: in the US it must win three separate approvals that can each say no; in Poland and India the government usually controls the path, and the hard part is the stages outside the lower house.

**United States: many doors, each with a lock.** Only a member of Congress can formally introduce a bill, even one the White House wrote. It goes to a **committee**, where most bills quietly die. If a committee reports it, the House majority leadership schedules a vote, and a simple majority passes it. In the Senate, most bills in practice need 60 votes to end debate, because of the [#filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_in_the_United_States_Senate). Both chambers must then pass **exactly the same text**, so differences are settled by a conference committee or by sending amendments back and forth. Only then does the bill go to the president, who has ten days (Sundays excepted) to sign or veto it. Tax bills must start in the House.

> The ten-day rule and the House's control of revenue bills were written at the [#Constitutional Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Convention_(United_States)) in Philadelphia in 1787.

**Poland: the government proposes, the Sejm decides.** Bills can come from the Council of Ministers, the president, the Senate, a group of 15 deputies, or 100,000 citizens, but government bills dominate. The Sejm debates each bill in **three readings** (czytania), with committee work between them, and passes it by a simple majority. The Senate then has 30 days; if it does nothing, the Sejm's text stands, and any Senate amendment or rejection can be overturned by an absolute majority in the Sejm. The president then has **21 days** to sign, veto, or send the act to the Constitutional Tribunal. A signed act takes effect only once it is published in the official journal, the **Dziennik Ustaw**. Budget bills and bills the government marks urgent run on shorter clocks.

> Today's procedure comes from the Constitution adopted in 1997 and approved by referendum that May.

**India: two houses, one tie-breaker.** An ordinary bill can start in either house and also goes through three readings, often with a stop at a standing or select committee. Both houses must pass it. If they deadlock, the president can call a **joint sitting**, where the Lok Sabha's larger numbers usually win; this has happened only three times, most recently for the [#Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevention_of_Terrorism_Act,_2002). **Money bills**, certified by the Speaker, can start only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha may suggest changes within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha can ignore. The president must assent to a money bill and can return other bills once, but must sign if Parliament passes them again. The Constitution sets no deadline for that decision, which once let President [@Zail Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zail_Singh) simply sit on a postal bill in 1986.

> The Constitution's lawmaking articles, 107 to 122, came into force on 26 January 1950.

**The pattern.** In Poland and India, a government with a lower-house majority can almost always get its bills through parliament, so the real checks come at the end: a president from a rival camp in Poland, an opposition-held upper house in India, and courts in both. In the US the checks are built into every step, so most bills die early and the ones that pass are usually the product of bargaining across both chambers and the White House. That is why lesson 7's veto matters so much more in Warsaw today than in Delhi.

items.example: The [#Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act) shows how hard the US rule of identical texts can bite. In late 2009 the House and Senate passed different health bills, and Democrats planned to merge them. Then [@Scott Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Brown_(politician)) won the [#2010 Massachusetts Senate special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_Senate_special_election_in_Massachusetts) in January, leaving Democrats with 59 votes, one short of ending a filibuster on a merged bill. Their workaround: the House passed the Senate's text unchanged, so no further Senate vote was needed, and President [@Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama) signed it in March 2010. The House's desired fixes went into a separate budget bill, the [#Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Care_and_Education_Reconciliation_Act_of_2010), which under Senate rules needed only a simple majority. In Poland or India, a majority government would simply have amended its own bill.

In India, part of the rules under the [#Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Personal_Data_Protection_Act,_2023) took effect today, a reminder that an act passed by Parliament often comes into force only in stages.

check.explain: In Poland the government usually commands the Sejm, which can override the Senate. In the US each step is a separate approval that can block the bill.

items.body:
Lessons 6 and 7 followed a law to the president's desk. Today's question is what happens after it is signed: who can say that a valid-looking law breaks the constitution, and throw it out? That power is called **judicial review**, and the three countries give it to very different bodies.

**United States: every court, one final word.** Article III of the Constitution creates "one supreme Court" and lets Congress set up lower federal courts, but it never says courts may strike down laws. The Supreme Court claimed that power itself in [#Marbury v. Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marbury_v._Madison) (1803), when Chief Justice [@John Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marshall) reasoned that a judge applying the law must prefer the Constitution when the two conflict. Because the power comes from ordinary judging, any federal or state judge can use it, but only in a real case brought by someone actually harmed. The nine justices, nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, serve for life and choose which appeals to hear. Today the Court has a 6–3 majority of justices appointed by Republican presidents.

> The Supreme Court first met in February 1790 at the Royal Exchange in New York, then the national capital.

**Poland: a special court for the constitution.** Poland follows the European model of a separate **constitutional court**. The **Constitutional Tribunal** (Trybunał Konstytucyjny) is not at the top of the ordinary courts; it does only one job: checking laws against the 1997 Constitution. Its 15 judges are elected by the Sejm for single nine-year terms. Cases come from the president (who can refer a law before signing, as lesson 7 noted), the prime minister, 50 deputies or 30 senators, any court with a doubt, and citizens through a **constitutional complaint**. Its rulings are final, but they take effect only when published in the **Dziennik Ustaw**. The separate **Supreme Court** (Sąd Najwyższy) is the top court for ordinary civil and criminal cases.

> The Tribunal was created by a 1982 constitutional amendment, passed under [#martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_in_Poland), and issued its first ruling in 1986.

That design has been the centre of a decade-long fight. In 2015 both the outgoing Civic Platform majority and the incoming PiS government chose judges for the same seats, and the court that emerged was widely criticised as captured by PiS. The [@Donald Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Tusk) government elected in 2023 treats it as improperly staffed and since 2024 has refused to publish its rulings. In 2026 the Sejm elected eight new judges; President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) swore in only three, and the dispute escalated into the [#2026 Polish Constitutional Tribunal crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Polish_Constitutional_Tribunal_crisis), with rival claims to lead the court. Each side says the other is breaking the constitution; there is no neutral referee, because the referee is the thing in dispute.

**India: one Supreme Court that does everything.** India's Supreme Court is both the final court of appeal and the guardian of the Constitution. Under Article 32, anyone whose fundamental rights are violated can go to it directly, and Article 13 expressly voids laws that breach those rights, so judicial review is written into the text. Judges are chosen largely by a **collegium** of senior judges. Most strikingly, in [#Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kesavananda_Bharati_v._State_of_Kerala) (1973), a 7–6 majority held that Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot destroy its **basic structure**: democracy, secularism, federalism, judicial review itself. No US or Polish court claims power over constitutional amendments.

> The Supreme Court of India held its first sitting on 28 January 1950, two days after the Constitution took effect.

**The pattern.** The US spreads review across all courts but limits it to real disputes; Poland concentrates it in one body, which makes that body a prize worth capturing; India concentrates it too but goes furthest, guarding even the constitution's core against amendment. Which model is wiser is still argued in all three countries.

items.example:
In 2014 Parliament passed, almost unanimously, the [#Ninety-ninth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-ninth_Amendment_of_the_Constitution_of_India) to replace the judges' collegium with a National Judicial Appointments Commission, which would have included the law minister and two "eminent persons" alongside senior judges. More than half of the state legislatures ratified it. In October 2015 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court struck it down by 4–1, holding that judicial independence is part of the basic structure and that giving politicians a say over appointments threatened it.

The case shows the Indian model at full strength: a court voided a constitutional amendment passed by both houses and the states. Supporters saw a defence of independent courts; critics, including many MPs, saw judges protecting their own power to choose their successors. In the US, by contrast, an amendment ratified by the states binds the Supreme Court, and in Poland the Tribunal cannot review amendments either.
items.inTheNews: Explaining his veto of Poland's law implementing the EU's [#Digital Services Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Services_Act), President [@Karol Nawrocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_Nawrocki) said he could not refer it to the Constitutional Tribunal because the Tribunal 'does not function', a direct result of the court crisis described above. In India, Yes Bank has asked the Supreme Court to review its own October judgment on AT-1 bonds, using the court's power to reconsider its final decisions.

check.q: Why can any US judge strike down a law, while in Poland only one body can?
options: The US Constitution lists every court that may do so
In the US review grew out of ordinary judging in real cases; Poland created a separate court just for constitutional questions
Polish ordinary courts are not allowed to read the Constitution
US judges are elected, so they have more legitimacy
check.explain: Marbury v. Madison tied review to deciding cases, so every court applies the Constitution; Poland follows the European model of one specialised constitutional court.

check.q: Which power does India's Supreme Court claim that neither the US Supreme Court nor Poland's Tribunal claims?
options: Hearing appeals in criminal cases
Striking down ordinary laws
Voiding a constitutional amendment that destroys the Constitution's basic structure
Advising the president
check.explain: Under Kesavananda Bharati (1973), amendments themselves can be struck down if they damage the basic structure, as happened to the judicial appointments amendment in 2015.

check.q: Why does the dispute over Poland's Tribunal matter for how laws are made, as seen in today's DSA veto?
options: The Tribunal must approve every bill before the Sejm votes
Without a Tribunal both sides accept, the president loses a usable alternative to the veto, and the government ignores the rulings it does issue
The Tribunal elects the president
The Tribunal can override a presidential veto
check.explain: Lesson 7 showed the president can refer a law instead of vetoing it; Nawrocki said that route was closed, and the government has not published Tribunal rulings since 2024.

items.recallQ: Why is Poland's Constitutional Tribunal a bigger political prize than any single US court, and how does India's basic structure doctrine go further than either?
items.recallA: Poland gives the power to strike down laws to one 15-member Tribunal elected by the Sejm, so whoever controls it controls constitutional review; in the US review is spread across all courts and limited to real cases. India's Supreme Court goes further still, claiming the power to void even constitutional amendments that damage the Constitution's basic structure.
